overview: The Medford Conservation Commission is responsible for protecting the city's natural resources through the enforcement of the Wetlands Protection Act and the review of development projects impacting resource areas. Its work from early 2023 through late 2026 includes permitting for regional dam improvements, managing invasive species in the Middlesex Fells, and overseeing the expansion of public waterfront access. The commission issues negative determinations of applicability and orders of conditions to ensure that construction projects include native plantings, erosion controls, and stormwater mitigation. At its most recent meeting, the commission was focused on finalizing certificates of compliance for state-managed projects and preparing for a formal review of new local wetlands regulations.

threads.name: South Reservoir Dam Improvements
threads.summary: The commission reviewed a major safety improvement project for the South Reservoir Dam submitted by the Town of Winchester. After discussing wetland impacts and tree removal, the commission approved an order of conditions requiring a one-to-three tree replication ratio and a pre-construction invasive species management plan. The project involved coordination with state and federal agencies regarding flood storage and riverfront areas.

threads.name: Shared-Use Paths and Waterfront Access
threads.summary: The commission has consistently supported the expansion of pedestrian and bicycle networks, starting with the Wellington Greenway extension and a bicycle path near the community gardens. A significant project involved the Route 28 pathway and boardwalk, which required detailed planting plans and alternatives to tropical hardwood for decking. By mid-2026, the commission was conducting pre-construction site visits to manage the removal of dead and diseased trees along these routes.

threads.name: Park and Recreation Improvements
threads.summary: The body manages environmental permitting for numerous city park renovations, including Phase 1 of the Carr Park project where conditions focused on knotweed management and construction debris removal. It also authorized dugout replacements at Veterans Memorial Park and lighting installations at the Condon Hatch Shell. The commission frequently monitors these sites for compliance before issuing final certificates to close out the permits.

threads.name: Large-Scale Residential Redevelopment
threads.summary: Major residential projects under commission review included a 40B development at 4000 Mystic Valley Parkway and the redevelopment of the former KISS 108 site on Revere Beach Parkway. For the latter, the commission mandated public greenway access, habitat enhancements, and the use of porous pavement to manage stormwater. These projects often required the applicant to provide additional data on seasonal high groundwater levels before receiving approval.

threads.name: Small-Scale Residential Compliance
threads.summary: The commission handles frequent requests for residential additions, retaining walls, and driveway replacements near wetlands, such as at Arlington Street and Winford Way. Common requirements for these approvals include the use of native seed mixes, the installation of permanent wetland markers, and the prohibition of non-native vegetation. The commission also performs site visits to verify that plantings meet the original orders of conditions before issuing certificates of compliance.

threads.name: Invasive Species and Habitat Restoration
threads.summary: Managing native habitats is a recurring priority, highlighted by the approval of a five-year vegetation management plan for the MBTA commuter rail right-of-way. The commission also authorized invasive plant management and pollinator habitat restoration at the Middlesex Fells Reservation's 90-millimeter meadow. Recent work includes bridge replacements and erosion remediation on Fells trails to protect local stream crossings.

threads.name: Local Wetlands Protection Regulations
threads.summary: In 2026, the commission began a section-by-section review of a new 42-page draft of local wetlands protection regulations. The draft proposes stricter standards than state law, including a two-to-one wetland replication ratio and a 25-foot no-activity buffer zone. Commissioners have debated various provisions, such as banning coal tar-based drive sealants and implementing tree replacement formulas for developers.
